questions.stem: A 4-year-old has a sudden high fever, is drooling, sits leaning forward with the neck extended and has muffled speech. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Keep the child calm, avoid examining the throat and prepare for emergency airway management
Look in the throat with a tongue blade
Lay the child flat for an exam
Obtain a throat culture right away

rationale.correct: Epiglottitis: drooling, dysphagia, distress and tripod position; nothing in the mouth and have airway equipment ready.

perOption.a: This suggests epiglottitis; examining the throat can trigger complete obstruction.
perOption.b: This can cause laryngospasm and airway obstruction.
perOption.c: Let the child keep the position of comfort.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Select the 3 findings most consistent with epiglottitis.

options.text: Sitting upright and leaning forward (tripod position)
Low-grade fever with a runny nose

rationale.correct: Epiglottitis: the 3 D's (drooling, dysphagia, distress), sudden high fever and tripod position.

perOption.a: Painful swallowing leads to drooling.
perOption.b: Epiglottitis is a rapidly progressing bacterial infection.
perOption.c: This position helps keep the airway open.
perOption.f: This fits viral croup or a cold.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate which condition it is most consistent with.

rows.text: Barking, seal-like cough that worsens at night
Infant with wheezing and large amounts of nasal secretions
Toxic appearance with sudden high fever

rationale.correct: Croup = bark and stridor; epiglottitis = drooling and toxicity; bronchiolitis = infant wheeze with secretions.

perOption.r1:c1: This is the classic croup cough.
perOption.r1:c2: Epiglottitis rarely causes a barking cough.
perOption.r2:c2: Swelling of the epiglottis makes swallowing painful.
perOption.r3:c3: RSV bronchiolitis causes wheezing and heavy secretions in infants.
perOption.r4:c1: Croup usually has a low-grade fever.
perOption.r4:c2: Epiglottitis is a rapid bacterial infection.
perOption.r4:c3: Bronchiolitis usually has a mild fever.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with croup has stridor at rest. Which treatment should the nurse expect?

options.text: Nebulized racemic epinephrine and a corticosteroid such as dexamethasone

rationale.correct: Croup: steroids for all; racemic epinephrine for stridor at rest. Watch for rebound after epinephrine.

perOption.a: These reduce airway swelling.
perOption.b: Croup is usually viral.
perOption.c: This isn't used for croup.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old with RSV bronchiolitis is having trouble feeding. Which intervention is most helpful?

rationale.correct: Bronchiolitis: nasal suctioning, hydration, oxygen if needed and contact precautions.

perOption.a: Infants breathe through the nose; clearing secretions makes feeding easier.
perOption.b: RSV is viral.
perOption.c: Elevating the head helps breathing.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A child with cystic fibrosis is prescribed pancrelipase. When should the child take it?

rationale.correct: Cystic fibrosis: enzymes with meals, a high-calorie, high-protein diet and fat-soluble vitamins.

perOption.a: Enzymes are needed to digest the fat and protein in food.
perOption.b: There's no food to digest then.
perOption.c: It is taken with every meal.
perOption.d: It is taken with all food.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: When should chest physiotherapy be scheduled for a child with cystic fibrosis?

rationale.correct: CF airway clearance: daily, before meals, often after a bronchodilator.

perOption.a: Doing it before meals clears the airways and reduces vomiting.
perOption.b: This may cause vomiting.
perOption.c: It is done daily.
perOption.d: It is usually done several times a day.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: Which test is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis?

rationale.correct: A sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher supports a diagnosis of CF.

perOption.a: High sweat chloride is diagnostic.
perOption.b: This isn't diagnostic.
perOption.c: This isn't diagnostic.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A 7-month-old is choking and can't cry or cough. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts, repeating as needed
Hold the infant upside down by the feet

rationale.correct: Infant choking: back blows and chest thrusts; start CPR if the infant becomes unresponsive.

perOption.a: This is the technique for infants under 1 year.
perOption.b: Abdominal thrusts can injure an infant's organs.
perOption.c: This can push the object deeper.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which finding is often an early sign of respiratory distress in a child?

rationale.correct: Early: tachypnea, tachycardia, restlessness, retractions. Late: bradycardia, cyanosis, lethargy.

perOption.a: Fast breathing and restlessness appear early as the child compensates.
perOption.b: This is a late, ominous sign.
perOption.c: This is late.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize early respiratory distress in children.

questions.stem: After a tonsillectomy, which finding most suggests bleeding?

options.text: Low-grade fever on the first day

rationale.correct: Post-tonsillectomy bleeding: frequent swallowing, clearing the throat and vomiting bright red blood.

perOption.a: Children swallow blood that trickles down the throat.
perOption.b: This is expected.
perOption.c: This is common during healing.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A parent is caring for a child after a tonsillectomy. Which statement needs correction?

options.text: "I'll let him drink through a straw."
"I'll give acetaminophen for pain as directed."

rationale.correct: After tonsillectomy: no straws, no red fluids, soft cool foods and watch for bleeding.

perOption.a: This soothes the throat.
perOption.b: Straws can dislodge clots and cause bleeding.
perOption.c: Red fluids can look like blood.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which parent statement shows understanding of how to prevent ear infections in infants?

options.text: "I won't prop the bottle, and I'll hold my baby upright to feed."
"I'll put my baby to bed with a bottle."

rationale.correct: Reduce otitis media with upright feeding, breastfeeding, no smoke exposure and vaccines.

perOption.a: Feeding while lying flat lets fluid enter the short, horizontal eustachian tubes.
perOption.b: This increases ear infections and tooth decay.
perOption.c: Secondhand smoke exposure still increases risk.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A child has tympanostomy tubes. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Keep water out of the ears when bathing or swimming, as the provider directs
Clean the ears with cotton swabs every day
Remove the tubes at home if they itch
Expect the tubes to stay in for life

rationale.correct: Tympanostomy tubes: protect the ears from water per provider instructions and report drainage.

perOption.a: Water entering through the tubes can cause infection.
perOption.b: Swabs can damage the ears.
perOption.c: Tubes are never removed at home.
perOption.d: They usually fall out on their own.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which vital signs are within the normal range for a 6-month-old?

rationale.correct: Pediatric vital signs change with age; know the normal infant ranges.

perOption.a: Infants normally have a heart rate of about 100 to 160 and a respiratory rate of about 30 to 60.
perOption.b: These are adult values.
perOption.c: These are too high.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: How should a parent measure a liquid medication for a toddler?

options.text: With an oral syringe or dosing device marked in mL
By mixing it in a full bottle of milk

rationale.correct: Pediatric medications: give with an accurate oral syringe, directed into the side of the cheek.

perOption.a: Household spoons are inaccurate.
perOption.b: Spoons vary in size.
perOption.c: The child may not finish the bottle.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A hospitalized 18-month-old screams and cries when the parents leave. What does this behavior show?

options.text: The protest stage of separation anxiety, which is expected

rationale.correct: Separation anxiety stages: protest, despair, detachment. Encourage parents to stay and keep routines.

perOption.a: Protest is the first stage of separation anxiety in toddlers.
perOption.b: This is a normal response.
perOption.c: Detachment is the late stage, with apparent disinterest.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: Which tool should the nurse use to assess pain in a 1-year-old?

options.text: Asking the child to describe the pain

rationale.correct: Choose the pain scale by developmental level.

perOption.a: FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) suits preverbal children.
perOption.b: This is for older children and adults.
perOption.c: This is for children about 3 and older.

options.text: Speaking in full sentences of 6 to 8 words

rationale.correct: Language milestones: first words around 12 months, two-word phrases at 2 years, simple sentences at 3.

perOption.a: Two-word phrases are typical at 2 years.
perOption.b: This is typical of older children.
perOption.c: This is a delay.
perOption.d: This is typical of school age.

questions.stem: Which statement by a parent of a 6-month-old shows a need for more teaching about nutrition?

options.text: "I'll add a little honey to the cereal for flavor."
"I'll introduce one new food at a time."

rationale.correct: No honey before 12 months; introduce single foods; no cow's milk as the main drink before 12 months.

perOption.a: This is appropriate around 6 months.
perOption.b: Honey can cause infant botulism before age 1.
perOption.c: This helps spot allergies.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Using the Holliday-Segar method (100 mL/kg for the first 10 kg, plus 50 mL/kg for each kg from 11 to 20), what is the daily maintenance fluid requirement for a 15 kg child?

rationale.correct: First 10 kg: 10 × 100 = 1,000 mL. Next 5 kg: 5 × 50 = 250 mL. Total = 1,250 mL/day.
references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
